prose_plain.lead_with: Start by naming the shame of feeling like a slow learner. Then tell them straight: the problem is how they're studying, not how smart they are. Say that before you teach them anything.
prose_plain.implication: These people have already tried studying harder and longer. It didn't work and they know it. So don't lead with tips. Lead with why their effort failed. Show them what was wrong with the approach, things like active recall or spaced repetition, and explain why grinding harder on a broken method gets you nowhere.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Learn and remember things faster so I can keep up with the people around me and stop feeling dumb
prose_plain.push: They hit a wall. Hours of studying, nothing sticks. No matter how much time they put in, they can't make progress. That's what drives them to look for something different.
prose_plain.pull: They want to know how a slow learner can learn faster. They're after a smarter, more efficient way to study.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared this is just who they are. That no technique will help because something is wrong with them at a deeper level.
prose_plain.habit: They keep studying the same way, just longer and harder. The same approach that's already failing them.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: Back your claims with science so people feel they're getting the real explanation, not another productivity hack. That cuts through the 'I'm just dumb' story they're telling themselves. Show them real people who used to struggle and don't anymore. And know that any technique you teach only works if they actually do it, so make it easy to turn into a habit.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: Some people search because they want out of pain. 'Rock bottom' and 'no hope left' and 'how do I quit drinking' are all someone screaming to escape a situation that is destroying them. Others search because someone they love is watching. 'Affecting their son' and 'be there for his kids and wife' are about protecting the people who matter most.
prose_plain.lead_with: Start where they actually are. They aren't looking for a polished program. They're on Day 1, or they are back on Day 1 again, and they feel completely alone. Meet them there.
prose_plain.implication: They have already tried willpower. They know 'just quit' doesn't work. So don't promise that. Instead, show them you understand the real reasons people fail: the lost social life, the first-week slip, the emptiness that hits when drinking is gone. Speak to those things directly.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: They want to stop drinking and then build a real life around being sober. Not just white-knuckle it. Actually feel like themselves again, keep the people they love, and not fall back into old patterns.
prose_plain.push: Something broke. A relationship took a hit. They came close to losing everything, maybe even their freedom. That's what pushed them to look for help.
prose_plain.pull: They believe sobriety could genuinely make their life better. They want encouragement. They want things to do that aren't drinking.
prose_plain.anxiety: The thing that scares them most is the emptiness. No friends. No social life. Depression settling in after they quit. The feeling that they lost drinking and gained nothing.
prose_plain.habit: Drinking was how they showed up in social situations. Without it they don't know what to do. And the pattern is the same every time: fine for a few days, then a slip.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: People in early recovery respond to others who have been exactly where they are. Saying 'I was there too' builds instant trust. When someone new says out loud that they are just starting, and others rally around them, that moment of belonging makes them more likely to stick with it.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: People in this market want to protect the people they love. They're yelling at their kids and they hate themselves for it. The guilt hits right after the anger does. Then the stress builds and the whole thing starts again. That cycle is what hurts most, not just the anger itself.
prose_plain.lead_with: Start by naming the cycle: anger, then guilt, then the fear of becoming a parent your kids are scared of. Say that out loud before you offer anything practical. People need to feel seen before they trust you enough to listen.
prose_plain.implication: Your buyers already know to breathe and count to ten. That isn't news. What they need is help with the moment before they snap, and with the guilt that keeps the cycle running after they do. Tip sheets won't cut it here.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: They want to stop yelling, especially at their kids. Not just in one moment, but for good. So the guilt stops. So they can feel like the parent they actually want to be.
prose_plain.push: They describe the anger, stress, and guilt as endless. One person called it extremely destructive. That word matters. This isn't mild frustration. They feel like something is broken.
prose_plain.pull: They want to turn the anger into something useful rather than something they regret. They want to put a stop to it, their words, not slow it down or manage it better. They want it gone.
prose_plain.anxiety: Some worry the anger is just who they are. They ask whether it is a mental health issue or simply their personality. That question underneath is: can I actually change, or am I stuck like this?
prose_plain.habit: They apologise after they blow up. Then they do it again. The apology feels like a reset but it isn't one. The pattern keeps repeating and they know it.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: Guilty parents trust someone who sounds credible and real. They respond strongly to other parents who were in the same place and got out of it. Seeing that someone else broke the cycle makes them believe they can too. The identity piece matters as well. They don't want to be that parent. That phrase carries real weight. Use it.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: Your clients are scared, not just stressed. They say things like 'I can't stop feeling anxious', 'I can't breathe', 'I can't focus on anything'. What they want most is simple: feel safe again and get through their day.
prose_plain.lead_with: Start by telling them you understand it never switches off. Acknowledge that 'why won't it just go away' feeling before you say anything about how you help. If you skip that, they won't trust the rest.
prose_plain.implication: The market is drowning in tips for calming down and coping. Your people have tried those. They cope, and the anxiety comes back anyway. That gap is your opening. Explain why anxiety keeps coming back even when someone is doing everything right. That explanation is what they haven't heard before.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: They aren't looking to feel slightly better. They want the constant anxiety to stop so they can think straight and get on with their life.
prose_plain.push: What pushed them to look for help: the anxiety got worse and they can no longer do basic daily tasks. It stopped being manageable.
prose_plain.pull: They don't want another coping tool. They want it gone. 'Why won't it go away' is the question sitting in their head when they find you.
prose_plain.anxiety: They worry that nothing will actually fix it because they have already tried coping and it hasn't worked. Deep down they fear this is just how they are now.
prose_plain.habit: Right now they white-knuckle their way through each day. They manage the symptoms just enough to function, but never break the cycle causing them.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They need to trust you before they buy. Show them you understand why anxiety keeps coming back, not just that it does. Share stories from people who felt the same and got real relief. And keep your tone calm and steady. A fearful person will click away the moment something feels pushy or clinical.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: Everything in this market points to romantic relationships. People want a relationship that works, or they want to stop hurting over one that ended. The pain they talk about most is the anxious-avoidant cycle and the grief of a breakup they can't let go of.
prose_plain.lead_with: These buyers already know the words. They've taken the quiz. They know if they're anxious or fearful-avoidant. So don't teach them the basics. Start with their exact pairing and give them a clear next step or decision. That's what gets their attention.
prose_plain.implication: This space is packed with attachment content. Everyone is saying roughly the same things. What cuts through is talking to them as one of their own. 'As an anxious person dating an avoidant' hits harder than any broad claim. Be specific about the situation, not first with a new idea.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: They want to understand their own style and their partner's, then either turn the relationship around or make peace with the fact that it's over.
prose_plain.push: The push is the cycle itself. The chasing, the shutting down, the feeling that someone is controlling them or guilt-tripping them into staying. It hurts and they're tired of it.
prose_plain.pull: They want to know if the pairing can actually work. They want to hear from someone who was anxious or avoidant and got through it. They're asking 'can this be healthy?' and 'how do you stop loving someone who pulls away?'
prose_plain.anxiety: Their biggest fear is that they're stuck. That their style, or the combination of styles, is just broken and nothing will fix it.
prose_plain.habit: They label themselves and their partners but don't change anything. The quiz becomes the answer instead of the start of something.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They trust people who know attachment theory properly, so expert framing matters. But what really moves them is someone who shares their exact label and came out the other side. A fellow anxious type who fixed their pattern carries more weight with this crowd than any credential.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: For people with bipolar disorder, staying alive and staying housed isn't a metaphor. It's the actual goal. A manic episode can cost someone their job. Losing a job can mean losing the roof over their head. When they say 'I have to survive', they mean it literally. Security and a stable place to live are what they are fighting for every day.
prose_plain.lead_with: They already know they have bipolar disorder. They're probably already on medication and seeing someone. Don't start there. Start with the part nobody has helped them with yet: how to hold a job, keep a relationship, and have a normal life on top of the treatment they are already doing.
prose_plain.implication: This market has heard 'medication and therapy' a hundred times. Saying it again won't move them. What will move them is showing them the practical tools: how to spot an episode before it takes over, how to track their moods, how to build a daily structure that holds when things get hard. That's what they haven't been given.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Hold my life together , keep a job, relationships, and stability , while managing an unpredictable mood disorder
prose_plain.push: A manic episode already cost them their job. They swing between rage and a depression that feels like nothing at all. That pattern is what broke their life and what they are terrified will break it again.
prose_plain.pull: They want to put their life back together while they are still struggling. They want to keep living, not just get through today.
prose_plain.anxiety: Deep down they believe the world is too unforgiving for someone like them. That stability is something other people get, not them. That they can't keep up, so why try.
prose_plain.habit: They move from crisis to crisis and deal with each one as it hits. There's no plan in place before the episode arrives. They're managing emergencies, not managing their condition.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They need to see people who actually have bipolar disorder and are living a functioning life. That cuts through hopelessness faster than anything else. They also need to trust that whoever is helping them knows what they are talking about, because this is a serious medical condition and they won't take advice from someone who doesn't seem credible.

They want to grow, but not at the cost of everything falling apart.
prose_plain.lead_with: These buyers already know they need to grow and get organised. They aren't looking for a reason to scale. They want to know how to do it without drowning in work or hiring a team before they are ready. Lead with that: growth that stays under control.
prose_plain.implication: This space is crowded. Generic 'grow your business' advice won't cut through. What will work is being specific about how to scale, whether that means delegation, written processes, or a clear framework for adding capacity without breaking what already works.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Go from solo freelancer to agency owner without burning out, hiring too soon, or losing control of the business.
prose_plain.push: They're overwhelmed by how much work lands on them. And they are scared of going back to the point where everything broke down before.
prose_plain.pull: They want to step up to agency owner, reach a bigger audience directly, and feel like they have actually made it to the next level.
prose_plain.anxiety: Moving too fast. Bringing on people before the business can support it, or not knowing which tasks they can safely hand off to someone else.
prose_plain.habit: Doing everything themselves. They genuinely can't see what they would give to another person. Delegation feels impossible because they have never done it.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: Buyers here trust coaches who have actually built an agency themselves, not just read about it. They also watch what businesses like theirs have done and follow that lead. And they respond well to a step-by-step approach, small commitments that build into bigger ones, rather than one big leap.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: Fear of the cancer coming back runs through almost everything these buyers say. Survival and relief from that fear are what they want most. They say it plainly: constant worry, anxiety after diagnosis, dread that it will return.
prose_plain.lead_with: Start by naming the fear they live with every day: what happens after chemo ends, and how lost and scared life feels once treatment is over. Then tell them a normal life is possible again. That's what gets their attention.
prose_plain.implication: Most marketing aimed at cancer survivors ignores what life actually feels like after treatment: scared, lost, not knowing what comes next. Because so few people talk about this directly, you have room to speak to it clearly and stand out.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Help me stop being afraid the cancer will come back and let me feel normal and enjoy my life again.
prose_plain.push: The constant dread that cancer will return, and the lost, confused feeling when chemo ends and everyone expects you to just move on.
prose_plain.pull: Feeling normal again. Coming back to life. Having fun. Seeing the world the way people who haven't been through this see it.
prose_plain.anxiety: They worry that if they relax and stop watching for signs, the cancer will come back. Letting their guard down feels dangerous.
prose_plain.habit: They stay on high alert all the time. Some reach for psychiatric medication just to stop the worry. Vigilance has become their default way of living.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They trust someone who has been through the same scare far more than a generic expert. They need to see other survivors who came out the other side. And given how medical and serious this all is, your credibility needs to be clear and real.

prose_plain.lead_with: Start by calling out the exact pain they are living with: the burnout, the resentment, the feeling that the person they used to be has gone, the fights with family. Then say out loud that wanting a life of your own isn't selfish. Say it clearly, before you say anything else. They need to hear that first. Only then do you talk about what you can do for them.
prose_plain.implication: Almost nothing out there speaks to the caregiver's own survival. Everything talks about how to care better for the parent. That's a wide open space. Make a bigger promise: that they can care well for their parent AND get their own life back. Don't skip straight to how it works. Earn their trust with the promise first.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: They want to care for their ageing parent without it destroying their marriage, their finances, their health, or their sense of who they are.
prose_plain.push: Caregiving has already taken a divorce, a house, and the person they used to be.
prose_plain.pull: A real way to set limits and still have a life, without walking away from their parent.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that setting limits makes them a bad child or an ungrateful one. They worry it will blow the family apart.
prose_plain.habit: They keep giving and giving because it feels like the only option. Stopping feels like abandoning someone who needs them.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They respond to someone who gets it because they have lived it too. They need to feel understood without being judged. And they need someone they respect to tell them clearly that it is okay to set limits.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: People feel their household is under threat. A partner's spending keeps blowing up the budget. Or one partner controls all the money and the other has to ask for basics. The relationship itself feels at risk.
prose_plain.lead_with: Start by telling them you get it. Their partner's money behaviour feels impossible to stop and impossible to live with. Say that out loud before you offer them any tools.
prose_plain.implication: There's no shortage of advice telling couples to 'just talk about money.' That advice ignores the real problem: one person has more power than the other. Show them a way to have that conversation that takes the power difference seriously.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: They want their partner to stop the harmful behaviour, or they want fair access to their own household money, and they want to do it without the relationship falling apart.
prose_plain.push: A partner whose spending never stops. Or three years of being refused money for personal needs. Something has got bad enough that they have to do something.
prose_plain.pull: They want to raise the subject without it turning into a fight. They want their partner to hear them instead of shutting them down.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared of the conflict itself. They have seen or lived through what happens when money arguments go wrong in a relationship.
prose_plain.habit: They bring it up. Their partner dismisses them, sometimes by saying they don't have an equal say. So they drop it. Then the same problem happens again.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They need actual words to use because they don't trust themselves to get it right in the moment. Hearing how other couples handled the same fight and what went wrong helps them feel less alone and more prepared. Framing it as two people on the same team instead of two people in a fight makes it easier for both sides to hear.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: These women say things like 'little family, no friends, no relationships' and ask 'how do I begin to live a life of my own.' That tells you they want to feel connected again and rebuild a real life after losing the identity they had as a parent.
prose_plain.lead_with: Start by naming what she lost. Her child was the centre of her world, and now that centre is gone. Say that out loud before anything else. Then tell her she can build a life that is truly hers. Only after that do you talk about how.
prose_plain.implication: Most of what is out there tells her to 'rediscover yourself,' which says nothing. You win by being specific. Show her what a rebuilt life actually looks and feels like, in concrete, human terms. Not a tagline. A picture.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Build a life and identity that are mine, now that my child no longer needs me at the centre of theirs.
prose_plain.push: I gave everything to my child and ended up with no friends, no relationships, and no idea who I am outside of being a parent.
prose_plain.pull: Feeling genuinely happy and fulfilled, living a life that is mine as an empty nester.
prose_plain.anxiety: That it is too late to start over, or that moving on means losing my purpose and my bond with my child.
prose_plain.habit: Keeping all her focus on her child, even when the child still lives at home, because being a parent is the only role she knows.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: She moves when she sees others who were in the same place and came out the other side. Real stories from real people who rebuilt themselves after the kids left. She also needs to feel understood, not pitied. Warmth and recognition matter more here than any clever argument.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: These buyers say 'I feel so lonely', 'I have no friends here', 'I don't belong anywhere', 'I miss my family'. What they want most is to feel at home and accepted somewhere.
prose_plain.lead_with: They can name what is wrong. They say loneliness, culture shock. But then they ask 'what should I do with myself?' So start there. Name the isolation. Tell them it is normal and it doesn't last forever.
prose_plain.implication: They already know what culture shock is. They have heard the word. What they don't have is a clear plan for getting through it. Give them that: a step-by-step path forward, a real way to start building friendships. That's what they will pay for.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Help me feel like I belong somewhere and make real connections, so I stop feeling lonely, homesick, and like I made a terrible mistake.

prose_plain.pull: Ways to get through culture shock, feel settled, and know how long it usually takes.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared they will never truly belong anywhere. They have already tried. They wonder if moving was a mistake.
prose_plain.habit: They pull back, stay home, replay it all in their head, and think about going back instead of putting roots down.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They trust someone who has felt exactly what they feel. They need to hear that other people got through this and how long it took. They respond to a coach who was once the lonely expat in the room.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: The biggest thing driving these buyers is guilt. They want to stop feeling it. They say things like 'stop feeling guilty', 'process guilt and shame without making it worse', and 'my mental health worsens when I talk to them'. They want to protect their peace. But they also feel the weight of what other people think, shown in phrases like 'abandoning my elderly parents'.
prose_plain.lead_with: Start with permission. Tell them they can stay estranged and still let go of the guilt. Show them how to work through it without having to go back. They have already chosen distance. What they need now is a way to carry it without it breaking them.
prose_plain.implication: They aren't seeing many other solutions for this specific problem. So you can make a strong promise. Promise peace without guilt. Make it clear that choosing estrangement can be the healthy thing to do. Own that angle.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Build a happy life away from a family that hurts them, without guilt and shame eating them alive.
prose_plain.push: Talking to their family makes their mental health worse. Contact isn't neutral for them. It causes harm.
prose_plain.pull: They want what a happy life away from a difficult family actually feels like. And they want to stop carrying the guilt of that choice.
prose_plain.anxiety: They worry about what people think. Are they a bad person for walking away from elderly parents? They also worry that trying to process it will stir everything up and leave them worse off.
prose_plain.habit: They keep drifting back into contact because the guilt gets too heavy. Or they stay stuck going around in circles with shame and never move forward.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They need to feel they aren't alone in this choice. Hearing from others who made the same call and came out okay makes it feel normal and safe. A qualified expert saying this is a valid, healthy decision gives them the confidence to trust it. And a coach who has lived something similar, or works only with people in this situation, signals that this person truly gets it.

Fatherhood.lf8_evidence: Core is the bond with his child ('don't feel a bond or connection to my first born son'); 'like parents are supposed to' and 'feeling disappointed for it' show shame against a social expectation.
Fatherhood.lead_with: Normalize and name it — 'Not feeling an instant bond with your baby doesn't make you a bad dad; it's common and it changes' — he experiences distress but doesn't know it's a known, solvable thing.
Fatherhood.implication: Almost nothing has been claimed to new dads on this; state the reassuring claim plainly and own the unaddressed problem.
Fatherhood.jtbd_job: Feel the love and connection to my baby I'm 'supposed' to feel — and stop feeling broken for not
Fatherhood.push: Four months in and 'still don't feel a bond' — quiet alarm and self-disappointment
Fatherhood.pull: Reassurance that the bond can grow plus concrete ways to build it
Fatherhood.anxiety: Fear that something is wrong with him as a father ('like parents are supposed to')
Fatherhood.habit: Staying silent about it because dads aren't 'supposed' to admit this
Fatherhood.cialdini_why: 'Other dads felt exactly this' relieves shame (Unity/Social Proof); a credible voice saying it's normal and fixable provides Authority for a man unsure where to turn.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: The deepest thing he wants is to feel close to his child. When he says he doesn't feel a bond with his son, and follows it with 'like parents are supposed to' and 'feeling disappointed,' that is shame talking. He is measuring himself against what he thinks a good dad feels, and he thinks he is failing.
prose_plain.lead_with: Tell him straight: not feeling an instant bond with your baby doesn't make you a bad dad. It's common. It changes. He is in real pain about this but he has no idea other dads go through the same thing or that it can get better. Say that plainly, first.
prose_plain.implication: Almost no one is talking to new dads about this. If you say it clearly and own it, you have the space to yourself. The reassurance alone is the offer.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Feel the love and closeness with his baby that he thinks he should feel, and stop feeling like something is wrong with him for not feeling it.
prose_plain.push: Four months in and still no bond. He isn't panicking out loud, but inside he is worried and ashamed of himself.
prose_plain.pull: He wants to hear that the bond can still grow, and he wants real, practical things he can do to build it.
prose_plain.anxiety: He is scared there is something wrong with him as a father. That phrase 'like parents are supposed to' tells you everything.
prose_plain.habit: He says nothing to anyone. Dads aren't supposed to admit this, so he carries it alone.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: Showing him that other dads felt exactly this takes the shame away. He isn't a broken outlier, he is in good company. And a voice he trusts telling him it is normal and fixable gives him something solid to hold onto when he has nowhere else to turn.

Fertility & trying to conceive.implication: Market is saturated with IVF/clinical claims; elaborate or differentiate the mechanism (natural/alternative or 'why your normal labs still mean something') rather than restate standard treatment.
Fertility & trying to conceive.jtbd_job: Get pregnant and become a parent after standard efforts have failed
Fertility & trying to conceive.push: 'My IVF failed after 3 years', 'still got a negative result last month' — devastation and time running out
Fertility & trying to conceive.pull: 'How can I get pregnant without IVF?' — a fresh route to the baby they want

Fertility & trying to conceive.cialdini_why: 'Did anyone have the same experience?' is explicit demand for peer stories (Social Proof); medical complexity requires credible authority; emotional rawness rewards an empathetic, liked voice.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: These women want a baby with every part of themselves. They say things like 'I can't get pregnant naturally' and 'we've been trying for three years.' That kind of want runs deep. They also ask a lot of questions and read everything they can find, because they are desperate to understand what is going wrong.
prose_plain.lead_with: They already know what IVF is. They have probably tried it. So don't sell them on the standard options. Show them something that worked when the standard options didn't. 'After failed IVF, here's what we did differently' or 'How I got pregnant without IVF' will stop them cold in a way that clinical talk never will.
prose_plain.implication: This space is crowded with the same clinical promises. If you say what every IVF clinic already says, you disappear. What gets attention is a different angle: a natural or alternative route, or an honest answer to why normal test results still leave women stuck. Give them that, and they listen.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Get pregnant and become a parent after the standard medical routes haven't worked
prose_plain.push: Failed IVF rounds. Another negative test last month. Time passing. These women aren't just frustrated. They're scared and heartbroken, and they feel the clock ticking.
prose_plain.pull: They want to know if there is another way. 'How can I get pregnant without IVF?' is a real question they type into search bars. They want a fresh path to the thing they want most.
prose_plain.anxiety: Their test results came back normal. All of them. That should be good news, but it isn't, because they still aren't pregnant. Normal results with no baby is its own kind of fear. If nothing is wrong, why isn't it working? That question haunts them.
prose_plain.habit: They keep going back to the same clinical process, round after round. Three failed IVF cycles and they are still waiting for the next one. They know it hasn't worked, but it's the only road they've been shown.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They ask things like 'did anyone else go through this?' They want to hear from real women who were in the same place. That matters more than statistics. They also need to trust whoever they are listening to, because the medical side of this is complicated and the emotional side is raw. A voice that is both credible and genuinely kind will earn that trust fast.

prose_plain.lead_with: Lead with the idea of never needing anyone again. That's the real promise. Make that the centre of everything. The guilt and the shame of depending on someone else are the feelings that push them to act. Speak to those first.
prose_plain.implication: A lot of coaches in this space talk about empowerment but leave it vague. Vague doesn't sell. Show a clear, real path to financial independence. And make sure your message speaks to who she wants to become, not just what she wants to do.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: She wants to become truly financially independent. She wants to make her own money and never have to rely on anyone. And she wants to stop feeling guilty about where she is right now.
prose_plain.push: She feels guilty, useless and even resentful about being financially dependent on someone else.
prose_plain.pull: She wants to be completely financially independent and make money on her own.
prose_plain.anxiety: She worries the path to financial independence means getting a regular nine-to-five job. That's something she wants to avoid.
prose_plain.habit: Right now she depends on a partner or family for money. She resents it. But she hasn't found a way out yet.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: These women strongly identify with being, or becoming, an independent woman. That shared identity is powerful. If you can show how you or someone like her got there, she pays attention. She wants a real person to look up to, not a brand.

prose_plain.lead_with: Open by naming the specific loneliness they feel every day. Something like: you love him but you are starving for touch, and you have started to wonder if something is wrong with you. They feel this in their chest. They just haven't heard anyone say it out loud yet.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: They want physical and emotional closeness back in their marriage. Or, if that is gone, they want out of the painful limbo. Either way, they don't want to lose the person they love.
prose_plain.push: For many, it has stopped being a bad patch and become a crisis. A partner asking for a divorce. Feeling miserable day after day. The dead bedroom is no longer something they are hoping will fix itself.
prose_plain.pull: They want to know what actually worked for someone else. They're asking 'what did you do to fix it?' They want to feel wanted again. That's the thing they are really chasing.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared it is already too late. And underneath that, they are scared the reason their partner pulled away is rejection or someone else. 'Is it safe to say she is cheating?' That fear sits just under the surface.
prose_plain.habit: They keep reaching for their partner and getting turned away. Then they pull back. Then they try again. This loop repeats. Being the one who always pursues, and always gets rejected, wears a person down.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're asking what worked for other people, so showing real stories of people who fixed this matters enormously. They're also dealing with something deeply personal, so they need to trust that the person helping them knows what they are talking about. And because the topic is so private, they will only open up to someone who doesn't judge them.

prose_plain.cialdini_why: Show them stories of real people who turned things around after 50 or 55. That answers 'how did someone actually do this' better than any promise you can make. They trust the person who restarted from the same bottom, not someone who never fell.

prose_plain.lead_with: They already know transition is hard. They're living it. What they don't know is why it hurts this much. Start there. Name the loss of identity, the loss of the tribe, the loss of the structure that told them who they were. Tell them that is the real reason it is so hard. Make them feel understood before you offer anything.
prose_plain.implication: Most of what is out there talks about reintegration in vague, generic terms. There's room to do something sharper. Name the specific things they lost: the structure, the purpose, the brotherhood. Say it plainly and say it more clearly than anything else they have read. That alone will make them feel seen.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Help me figure out who I am and where I belong now that the military's structure and my brothers are gone.
prose_plain.push: They feel useless. They feel alone. The adjustment hit harder and faster than they expected and they don't know what to do with that.
prose_plain.pull: They want to understand why this is so hard. And they want to see that other people got through it and came out the other side.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're afraid that struggling means something is wrong with them. Especially if they were never in combat. They think they should be fine. They aren't fine. And they are ashamed of that.
prose_plain.habit: They go quiet. They white-knuckle it on their own. They don't ask for help.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They trust people who served. If you get it, they will listen. Show them veterans who struggled and then found their footing. That reduces the shame of struggling. And lean into the brotherhood. They spent years in one of the tightest groups a person can belong to. That identity is still there. Speak to it.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: These buyers are in real pain. You see it in what they say: 'I feel hollow and empty and purposeless', 'I still hate myself', 'now I feel ugly and worthless'. That isn't frustration. That's someone whose sense of self has been gutted. Alongside that, they are desperate to feel liked and valued again. They keep craving the ex's approval. prose_plain.lead_with: Name the exact pain before you offer anything. Say it out loud: you went no contact and you still miss him, and you hate yourself for missing him. They already know it hurts. What they don't know is why it still hurts when they are doing what everyone told them to do. Start there. Name the specific agony first. Then you can talk about what helps.
prose_plain.implication: These buyers already know the words. Trauma bond. No contact. Discarded. They have read the posts and watched the videos. So don't explain what those words mean. They know. What they don't know is why no contact alone isn't working, and what actually breaks the hold. That's what your copy needs to answer. Go deeper into the why, not wider across the what.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Stop obsessing over the ex, get their self-worth back, and feel like themselves again.
prose_plain.push: No contact is supposed to be the answer. They're doing it. And it isn't working. The pain is still there months later. That's the thing pushing them to look for something more.
prose_plain.pull: They want a way to get the ex out of their head for good. And they want to like themselves again. That's what they are willing to pay for.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared they will cave. They say things like 'I always cave around the three-week mark'. And underneath that is a quieter fear: that nothing will ever actually work for them.
prose_plain.habit: When the pain spikes, they ruminate. They check up on the ex. They run the same self-blame loops on repeat. These habits feel like staying connected to something, even though that something is hurting them.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They want to know you understand exactly what happened to them, not just in general terms but specifically. That earns trust. They also look hard at other people's stories. When someone asks 'what made you stop blaming yourself?', they aren't making small talk. They need to see that recovery is real and that someone else got there. And they feel a strong bond with others who went through the same thing. They see themselves as a group. Speak to that.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: The pain here is raw. People say things like "it's torture, I just cry" and "I can't stand it anymore." That's not frustration. That's someone at breaking point. On top of that, they're terrified the thoughts mean something about who they are as a person. Thoughts about harming others, or being a predator, or being evil. They're not just scared of the thoughts. They're scared the thoughts prove they're a monster.
prose_plain.lead_with: They already know they have OCD. They've Googled it. They don't need you to explain what intrusive thoughts are. What they need is to believe there's a real way out. Start by showing them why everything they've tried hasn't worked, and that there's a specific approach that does. Give them a reason to trust the solution before you sell anything.
prose_plain.implication: These people have already tried pushing the thoughts away. It didn't work. So don't offer more of the same. Show them that fighting the thoughts makes them worse, and that the real fix is facing them in a particular way. Name the approach. Be specific about why it works. Vague promises of feeling better won't move them. A clear explanation of a real method will.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: They want the thoughts gone for good, not just managed. And they want to know, without any doubt, that having the thoughts doesn't make them a bad person.
prose_plain.push: The thoughts feel like torture. They cry. They say they can't take it anymore. Some can't study or think straight because the thoughts keep breaking through. That's what's driving them to look for help.
prose_plain.pull: They want it completely gone. Not reduced. Not coped with. Gone. They say things like "genuinely stop it" and "get rid of it forever." They want their life back, not a workaround.
prose_plain.anxiety: They worry that needing help proves the thoughts are real. That if they have to see a specialist for thinking about harming someone, maybe they really are dangerous. This fear can stop them reaching out at all.
prose_plain.habit: They keep asking others for reassurance that they're not evil. And they keep trying to push the thoughts out of their head. Both things feel like relief in the moment. Both things make it worse over time.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They need to see that real specialists treat this, and that it responds to treatment. That makes it feel less like a character flaw and more like a condition. They also need to hear that other people with the same horrifying thoughts got better. That breaks the shame. It tells them they're not uniquely broken.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: Your buyers want to feel like winners. They want to be the person who gets things done, who hits goals, who doesn't let the day slip away. Underneath that is a quieter pain: the guilt of knowing they wasted another afternoon. They don't just want to be more productive. They want to stop feeling bad about themselves.
prose_plain.lead_with: Start with what they already know: they know what they need to do, and they still don't do it. That's the sore spot. Don't offer another technique to learn. Show them something that takes what they already know and actually gets it done.
prose_plain.implication: These buyers have heard of Pomodoro. They've tried time-blocking. They've read about deep work. Pitching those again will lose them fast. What they haven't figured out is why their brain keeps pulling them toward easy, pointless tasks instead of the real work. Speak to that. Explain what's actually happening in their head, and why your approach fixes it when the other things didn't.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Stop wasting time and reliably do the work I already know I should be doing
prose_plain.push: They lose time in small chunks, all day, every day. They want to focus. They try to focus. Then they look up and an hour is gone. The desire to do well is real. The follow-through keeps failing.
prose_plain.pull: They want to feel locked in. Focused. Productive in a way that feels almost effortless. The word they use is 'insane productivity' because what they want feels that far from where they are now.
prose_plain.anxiety: They've bought planners. They've downloaded apps. They've made lists about their lists. The fear is that your thing becomes one more item on the list that never gets done.
prose_plain.habit: They write to-do lists constantly. They tick off the quick, easy tasks first because it feels good. The hard, important work stays at the bottom. The list grows. The real work doesn't get done.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They want to hear that someone cracked this, and that it wasn't just willpower. They respond to an expert who has a real system, not generic advice. They want clear boundaries around their time, like set end points and firm commitments, because that structure is what they're missing. And they want to know other people have actually escaped this pattern. That proof matters to them.

prose_plain.anxiety: They're afraid it's going to be hell. They've relapsed before. And they worry that one cigarette from a friend, one bad day, and they'll be back where they started.
prose_plain.habit: Reaching for a cigarette or vape is automatic. It happens from routine and social situations before they even think about it. And they've told themselves so many times that quitting is too hard that they almost believe it.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: Show them real stories of ordinary people who quit without it being a nightmare. That makes it feel possible, not just for special people with iron willpower. And get them to make a small commitment early, because once someone says out loud they're doing this, they're far more likely to follow through.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: They want a comfortable life and financial freedom. But fear is loud too. They talk about being scared to invest, watching others lose money, and getting stuck overthinking every decision before they even start.
prose_plain.lead_with: They've already picked real estate. So don't sell them on why real estate. Speak to the two things stopping them: fear, and not having much money to start with.
prose_plain.implication: This space is full of gurus and no-money-down promises. Your buyers have heard it all. Don't just promise passive income again. Show them a clear, specific way to do it that feels safe enough to actually try.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Do their first deal and start building passive income, even with little money and a lot of fear.
prose_plain.push: Real estate feels overwhelming. They can't make themselves pull the trigger, so they just keep researching and going nowhere.
prose_plain.pull: Passive income. Financial freedom. And the hope that there's a real way to start without a lot of money.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared of losing money. They've seen it happen to others and they don't want it to happen to them.
prose_plain.habit: They stay stuck. More research, more podcasts, more thinking about it. The first deal never happens.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They trust people who have already done it, so a real track record matters more than credentials. Hearing how someone else closed their first deal makes it feel possible for them. And when a deal or a market looks like it won't wait, it pushes them to stop sitting on their hands.

Recovery from redundancy / job loss.lead_with: They're in acute pain/shame and panic; lead with stabilizing the emotional hit ('this is grief, not failure') AND the immediate practical next step.
Recovery from redundancy / job loss.implication: Few credible offers speak to the emotional recovery specifically; enlarge the claim — recover your identity and income, not just 'find a job.'
Recovery from redundancy / job loss.jtbd_job: Get back on my feet — rebuild income and self-worth after being let go.
Recovery from redundancy / job loss.push: Devastation, guilt, and immediate financial crisis after losing the job.
Recovery from redundancy / job loss.pull: A path to a new job and feeling like a capable person again.
Recovery from redundancy / job loss.anxiety: What if I try hard again and still fail / stay worthless (already 'worked so hard' with no result).
Recovery from redundancy / job loss.habit: Spiral in shame and 'giving up' because the loss feels like losing part of yourself.
Recovery from redundancy / job loss.cialdini_why: Social Proof: stories of others who bounced back restore hope; Authority: credible guidance reduces panic during crisis; Liking: empathy ('I've been there') opens a shame-shut person up.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: Some people in this market have no food, no money, and no way to pay their bills. Some are back living with their parents. That's basic survival. On top of that, many feel like a failure or worthless. That's about who they think they are, not just what they have in the bank.
prose_plain.lead_with: These people are in pain and panic at the same time. Start by telling them this is grief, not a character flaw. Then give them one concrete thing to do right now. They need both. Either one without the other won't hold their attention.
prose_plain.implication: Most offers in this space just promise to help people find a job. That leaves a door wide open. Speak to the identity hit as well as the income hit. The person who buys wants to feel like themselves again, not just employed again.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Get back on my feet. Rebuild my income and my sense of self after losing my job.
prose_plain.push: The devastation of losing the job, the guilt that comes with it, and the financial pressure that starts immediately.
prose_plain.pull: A new job and feeling like a capable person again.
prose_plain.anxiety: I worked hard before and it still went wrong. What if I try again and fail again? What if this is just who I am?
prose_plain.habit: Spiral into shame and stop trying, because losing the job feels like losing part of who they are.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: Stories of people who bounced back give them hope that it is possible for them too. A calm, credible voice cuts through the panic. And if you show real empathy, people who are shut down with shame will actually open up and listen.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: People say things like 'I went from always having someone home to nobody' and 'at 55 I want to feel loved before I go.' That tells you companionship is what they are really after. Others say they feel 'lonely and lost' or talk about a 'last straw' or an affair. That tells you they are in pain and want a way out.
prose_plain.lead_with: Before you offer anything, show them you understand what it feels like to go from a full house to an empty one. Name that loneliness out loud. Once they feel heard, they will listen to what comes next.
prose_plain.implication: Your buyers are split. Some want to save the marriage. Some have already decided it is over. Speak to both, but don't try to say the same thing to both at once. What cuts through is giving their specific situation a name. Words like 'narcissist' or 'no contact' tell a person 'that is exactly what I am dealing with.' Generic relationship advice doesn't do that.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Make sense of a marriage that is broken or ending, then get through it and build a life where I feel loved again.
prose_plain.push: The feeling that 'we don't love each other anymore,' the sense that 'it isn't healthy,' and whatever finally became the last straw.
prose_plain.pull: They want to feel like themselves again, feel loved while they still can, and be able to move on without looking back.
prose_plain.anxiety: Life feels blank and they don't know where to begin. They also worry about being blamed, whether by their parents or their spouse.
prose_plain.habit: They keep staying and trying to talk it through, even though their spouse never really hears them. They go back to the same conversation hoping this time will be different.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: When people see words like 'STBX' or 'no contact,' they recognise their own world and feel less alone. Hearing other people's 'last straw' stories makes leaving feel normal rather than shameful. A calm, knowledgeable voice matters too, because these buyers feel lost and want someone who actually knows the way.

The unmet hardwired need is companionship and a livable, connected life (a comfortable existence and human belonging) rather than the romanticized location-freedom the niche markets.
Remote work & digital nomad life.lead_with: Name the loneliness/isolation of remote work precisely before pitching any community, coliving, or routine fix.
Remote work & digital nomad life.implication: The 'work from anywhere' promise is saturated, but the loneliness sub-problem is under-claimed; lead with a unique mechanism for built-in connection (coliving/coworking, structured social design), not a bigger freedom promise.
Remote work & digital nomad life.jtbd_job: Keep my remote/nomad freedom while feeling connected, seen, and not isolated.
Remote work & digital nomad life.push: 'I feel like I'm disappearing... I no longer have friends' — acute isolation while working alone.
Remote work & digital nomad life.pull: Structured belonging — 'coliving coworking programs', getting 'connected with people'.
Remote work & digital nomad life.anxiety: That a fix means giving up the autonomy/lifestyle they chose, or that forced community feels fake.
Remote work & digital nomad life.habit: Defaulting to staying home/online, telling themselves the freedom is worth the loneliness.
Remote work & digital nomad life.cialdini_why: Belonging is the core need, so 'people like me, together' (Unity) and seeing peers who solved isolation (Social Proof) move them; warmth/relatability (Liking) lowers the barrier to a lonely audience.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: What buyers talk about most isn't freedom or travel. It's loneliness. They ask whether the nomad life is lonely. They say things like 'I feel like I'm disappearing' and 'I no longer have friends.' What they actually want, underneath all of it, is to feel connected and to have a real life with real people around them. That's the need this market isn't getting met.
prose_plain.lead_with: Name the loneliness exactly as it feels before you mention any fix. Say it out loud before you talk about community, coliving, or building a routine.
prose_plain.implication: Everyone in this space promises freedom and flexibility. That promise is worn out. But almost nobody is talking directly about the loneliness. If you lead with that and show a clear way to feel connected built into how you work and live, you stand apart without needing a bigger or louder freedom promise.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Keep my remote life and my freedom, but stop feeling invisible and alone while I live it.
prose_plain.push: The feeling that you are disappearing. That you are working alone every day and the friendships are gone.
prose_plain.pull: A life where connection is already built in. Coliving, coworking, programs that put real people around you.
prose_plain.anxiety: That fixing the loneliness means giving up the freedom they worked hard to get. Or that any group will feel forced and fake.
prose_plain.habit: Staying home, staying online, and telling themselves the lifestyle is worth the loneliness.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: These buyers are lonely, so what moves them is seeing people like them who found their way through it. Show real people who solved the same problem. Be warm and easy to relate to. A cold or polished pitch pushes a lonely audience further away.

Retirement & FIRE.implication: FIRE concepts are well-worn; strengthen the mechanism (specific savings-rate math, sequencing) and segment by life stage (e.g., 'starting at 48').
Retirement & FIRE.jtbd_job: Reach a secure retirement (or early independence) without fear of running out, even if I'm behind.

prose_plain.implication: FIRE isn't a new idea to these people. They have heard the basics. What wins them over is the specific detail , the exact numbers, the right order of steps , and content that speaks to their stage of life, like starting fresh at 48.

prose_plain.habit: They have tried before and stopped. When someone asks 'how do I save money again', that word again says everything , this isn't the first attempt.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: Money and retirement are high stakes, so they need to trust who they are listening to. They also want to see real people who did it, not just theory , asking how others saved enough shows they want proof that is relatable, not just expert. prose_plain.cialdini_why: Show them people who went back and were fine. That proves it can be done. Be warm about the fear and the hard experiences they have had. That earns trust. Then give clear, grounded guidance on readiness and the return itself.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: Your clients want to keep more of what they earn. That's the whole game. They feel the pain of paying more tax as a self-employed person than they did as an employee, sometimes on the same income or less. That stings. They also carry a quiet dread of getting it wrong. Filing wrong. Missing something. Owing more than they should. So two things drive them: wanting more money in their pocket, and wanting to stop worrying they are doing it wrong.
prose_plain.lead_with: They already know they are overpaying. You don't need to convince them of the problem. Lead with the specific thing that fixes it. Show them how self-employed people legally cut their tax bill. The more specific the better.
prose_plain.implication: Plenty of people say 'save on taxes.' That promise is so common it stops meaning anything. What cuts through is naming the exact thing you use to save the money. An S-corp election. A deduction most self-employed people miss. The specific thing builds belief. A vague promise doesn't.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: They want to stop paying more tax than they did as an employee and get their bill as low as the law allows.
prose_plain.push: They're asking themselves: why am I paying more tax now than when I had a regular job, even though I am not earning more? That question is sitting in their head. It's your opening.
prose_plain.pull: They're searching for a legal way to pay less self-employment tax. That's the outcome they want. Speak to that directly.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared of getting it wrong. Filing wrong, triggering an audit, or missing something they should have caught. Some aren't even sure if they owe what they have been told they owe.
prose_plain.habit: Right now they file their taxes without any real strategy. They pay the bill because they assume that is just what it costs to be self-employed. Nobody told them there was another way, so they never looked.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: People don't hand money or legal decisions to someone they don't trust. So your credentials matter. CPA, tax professional, whatever proves you know what you are doing. Show them people like them who paid less. Concrete numbers from real clients. And remind them that tax deadlines are real. Year-end comes whether they act or not.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: The pain these people feel is social. They see a friend get engaged and feel a knot in their stomach. They hear the family questions and want to disappear. They lie awake thinking 'what is wrong with me?' That is the wound. They aren't looking for love tips. They want to stop feeling broken every time someone else gets a ring.
prose_plain.lead_with: Start with that ache. The comparing yourself to married friends. The pressure from family. The feeling that everyone else got the memo and you missed it. Then tell them there is a way to feel genuinely happy on their own that doesn't collapse the moment another wedding invite lands on the mat.
prose_plain.implication: They have already heard 'love yourself' a hundred times. It didn't stick. If your message sounds like that, they will scroll past it. You need to show them something they haven't tried, a real way to build contentment that holds up even on the hard days when the comparison hits hard.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: They want to feel happy, whole, and at peace being single. Not just okay with it. Actually good. They want to stop flinching when someone announces an engagement.
prose_plain.push: Everyone around them is getting married and they are still alone. That comparison is what tips them from discomfort into action.
prose_plain.pull: They want to enjoy their own company. They want to stop feeling like something is missing. They're asking themselves, quietly, whether it is possible to be genuinely happy single.
prose_plain.anxiety: They worry that making peace with being single means giving up on ever finding someone. They also worry the good feeling won't last. They have had okay days before. They know the bad days come back.
prose_plain.habit: They scroll dating apps that go nowhere but keep going back. And they have absorbed a lifetime of the message that being with someone is what makes a person complete.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: When they see real people who are single and actually happy, not performing happiness, it starts to feel possible for them too. Being welcomed into a group of people who chose this path gives them somewhere to belong that isn't the couples table. And a coach who doesn't make them feel stupid or broken for being single in their twenties will earn their trust fast.

prose_plain.habit: They carry it alone. No one believes them. And they have nothing that actually helps when a flashback hits.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They need to trust you before they will listen to you. That trust comes from showing you understand trauma, not just know about it. Hearing from people who had the same experience and got through it answers the question they are really asking: can someone like me recover?

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: Writers here are scared people will judge their work and find it bad. They worry they have no right to write at all. But underneath that fear is a real hunger: they want to prove, to themselves more than anyone, that they can finish a book and put it into the world. That matters to them deeply.
prose_plain.lead_with: These writers already know they should push through. They don't need convincing that writing is worth doing. What they need is a clear process that gets the draft finished even on the days when doubt is loud. Lead with that.
prose_plain.implication: 'Just keep writing' is advice every writer has already heard a hundred times. It doesn't help them. Give them a specific way to stay consistent and break through blocks, something that makes finishing feel like the natural result rather than a distant hope.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Actually finish the book I started, instead of stalling at chapter one.
prose_plain.push: Stuck in the middle of a project, no momentum, and a quiet voice telling them they can't do this.
prose_plain.pull: A finished manuscript they feel good about.
prose_plain.anxiety: What if I finish it and nobody reads it? What if finishing it just proves I was never good enough to write it?
prose_plain.habit: They wait until they feel ready or inspired. That feeling rarely comes. So the book sits there.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: Writers trust guidance from someone who has actually published. They also respond to small daily writing commitments because those small wins build a new story about who they are: someone who finishes. Seeing other stuck writers who did finish gives them permission to believe they can too.
